questions.prompt: In the Draft vs Final pattern, a background autosave runs and later the user clicks **Save**. What does each one do to the `TaskItem`?
options: Autosave sets `IsDraft = false`; Save sets `IsDraft = true`
Only Save calls `SaveChangesAsync()`; autosave stays in memory
Autosave saves with `IsDraft = true`; Save sets `IsDraft = false`
Both save the same way; `IsDraft` is only used for the UI text
questions.explanation: A background save without explicit user intent must be treated as a draft: autosave marks `IsDraft = true` and records `LastAutoSavedAt`, while the explicit Save sets `IsDraft = false`, meaning the user has confirmed the data.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson call `<TextBox Text="{Binding Task.Description}" />` wrong in an app with autosave?
options: It binds the EF entity directly instead of ViewModel state
A TextBox cannot bind to a nested property path like that
It silently makes the binding OneTime instead of TwoWay
EF Core entities cannot be displayed by WPF controls at all
questions.explanation: Binding the EF entity directly is dangerous. The production approach binds to ViewModel state (`EditableDescription`), so you edit ViewModel state, not the EF entity.

questions.prompt: `IRepository<>` and `AppDbContext` are registered as scoped. Inside a background service you call `_scopeFactory.CreateScope()` and resolve `IRepository<MyEntity>` from it. Why do `GetAllAsync()`, an edit and `SaveChangesAsync()` all work together?
options: Scoped services behave like singletons inside background services
Each `GetRequiredService` call copies state into a new DbContext
`SaveChangesAsync()` re-reads entities from the database first
The scope returns the same repository and the same DbContext
questions.explanation: Within one scope the DI container creates a scoped service once and returns that same instance afterwards. The repository and its DbContext are shared, so the entity loaded by `GetAllAsync` is tracked by the same context that `SaveChangesAsync` uses.

questions.prompt: Code after `_host.StartAsync()` never runs, and nothing explains why. What does the lesson call the single most important fix to keep permanently?
options: Commenting out every hosted service and leaving them disabled
Turning on `ValidateOnBuild` (and `ValidateScopes`) for the host
Calling `StartAsync()` from a ViewModel instead of `App.xaml.cs`
Lowering the Serilog minimum level to `Verbose` permanently
questions.explanation: Without build-time validation, a missing or broken registration can fail silently when the host starts. With `ValidateOnBuild` you immediately get errors such as "Unable to resolve service for type 'IMessageBusService' while attempting to activate 'AutoSaveBackgroundService'".

source.section: ✅ METHOD 1 (BEST): Force DI validation at build time

questions.prompt: WPF has no automatic request scope like ASP.NET Core. Where does the lesson say is the best place to create a scope for scoped services such as DbContext?
options: In the WindowService: one scope per window, disposed on `Closed`
In `App.OnStartup`: one scope kept for the app's whole lifetime
In every property getter that needs to use the DbContext
Nowhere; register the DbContext as a singleton instead
questions.explanation: A window has a clear lifetime, so the WindowService creates a scope per window, resolves the window from it, and disposes the scope on `Closed`: a per-window unit of work with automatic disposal.

source.section: BEST PLACES to create scopes (in order)

options: `Configure<T>` cannot bind a configuration section at all
`AddOptions<T>` registers the settings class as a scoped service
It can chain `ValidateDataAnnotations()` and `ValidateOnStart()`
`AddOptions<T>` reloads the settings file on every read
questions.explanation: Both bind the section the same way, but `AddOptions<T>()` returns an `OptionsBuilder<T>` that unlocks validation and `ValidateOnStart()`, so the app fails fast at startup if the config is invalid.
